You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

=== TEXT A ===
We spent three months building a feature nobody asked for.

It was elegant. It was well-engineered. It shipped on time. And in the first 90 days, almost no one used it.

I still remember the launch thread. Screenshots. Confetti emoji. A demo that made the product look smarter than it actually was. We told ourselves we were being proactive — solving a problem users would have eventually. We had internal data. We had a slide that said “high intent.” We had conviction.

What we did not have was a single person who had said, “I need this.”

The usage graph was a flat line with a few polite clicks from people on our team. Support tickets did not mention it. Sales did not sell it. Power users found workarounds around it, which is a polite way of saying they ignored it.

The hard part was not the wasted engineering time. It was the story we had to tell ourselves afterward. We had not failed because we shipped slowly. We had failed because we shipped a solution in search of a problem.

Here is what I learned, and what I still repeat in kickoffs:

1. Usage is the only honest launch metric. Applause is not a metric. “Looks great in the demo” is not a metric. If the feature does not change a weekly habit, it did not ship. It just deployed.

2. “Nobody asked for it” is not automatically a virtue. Sometimes users cannot articulate the next step. Often they can. We skipped the unglamorous work: five conversations, a prototype, a fake door, a waitlist. We protected our idea from contact with reality.

3. Beautiful unused features have a cost beyond the sprint. They add surface area, docs, edge cases, and cognitive load. Every unused control is a tax on the people who actually use the product.

4. Kill criteria should be written before the build, not after the embarrassment. We should have said: if fewer than X people complete this flow in 30 days, we remove it. Sunsetting something you were proud of is cheaper than carrying it forever.

5. The team did not fail. The process did. Smart people will fill a vacuum of evidence with taste and optimism. That is not a character flaw. It is a design problem for how you decide what to build.

I used to think shipping was the brave part. Now I think the brave part is admitting a feature is a hypothesis, not a gift. Talk to users before you write the ticket. Instrument the thing you think they will do. Be willing to delete your favorite screen.

If you have a feature sitting at 2% adoption and a roadmap full of “phase 2,” that is not momentum. That is inventory.

What is a feature you shipped that the data quietly retired? I would rather hear that story than another launch post.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Last year I spent six weeks building a feature that exactly four people used. Two of them were on my team.

Here's what happened, and the lesson I'm still chewing on.

We had a dashboard. Customers kept telling us they wanted to "customize" it. So we built a full customization layer: drag-and-drop widgets, saved layouts, per-user preferences, the works. It was clean. It was tested. The demo went beautifully.

Then we shipped it, and nothing happened.

Not a spike. Not a trickle. Analytics showed a handful of people opened the customization panel, poked at it, and left their layout exactly as it was. Thirty days in, adoption was under 1%.

My first instinct was to blame discoverability. Add a tooltip. Add an onboarding nudge. Send an email. We did all three. Adoption barely moved.

So I finally did what I should have done at the start: I called the people who had asked for it.

What I learned in those conversations was uncomfortable. When customers said they wanted to "customize the dashboard," almost none of them meant they wanted to rearrange it. They meant one specific number was buried three clicks deep and they wanted it on the front page. Different customers wanted different numbers, so it sounded like a customization problem. It wasn't. It was an information hierarchy problem wearing a customization costume.

We had translated a symptom into a solution and skipped the diagnosis entirely.

The real fix took about four days: surface the top handful of metrics people actually cared about, based on usage data, and make them prominent by default. That change got used by nearly everyone, because it required nothing from them.

Here's the lesson I took away, and it's not "talk to your users." Everyone says that. We *did* talk to our users. We just listened to their proposed solution instead of their underlying problem.

The lesson is this: when someone requests a feature, the request is data about their pain, not a spec. "I want X" almost always means "I'm frustrated by Y, and X is the first thing I could imagine that would make Y go away." Your job is to find Y. If you build X without understanding Y, you might get lucky. But you're gambling six weeks on it.

A few things I now do differently:

Before scoping anything, I ask "what would you do with this once you had it?" The answer is usually more revealing than the request itself.

I look for the smallest possible version that tests whether the problem is real. Sometimes that's a manual workaround. Sometimes it's a mockup. It's almost never the full build.

I treat low adoption as information, not failure. The feature nobody used taught me more about our customers than most of the features that worked.

I still think about those four users sometimes. I hope they enjoyed their widgets.

What's a feature you built that nobody touched, and what did it teach you?
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: numbered list where prose was asked for
negative parallelism - 'It did not ship. It just deployed' / 'That is not momentum. That is inventory'
short punchy triad opener - 'It was elegant. It was well-engineered. It shipped on time.'
generic anecdote with no specific product detail
tells_B: signposting - 'Here's what happened' / 'Here's the lesson I took away'
triad of short fragments - 'It was clean. It was tested. The demo went beautifully.'
relentless short fragments - 'Not a spike. Not a trickle.' / 'Add a tooltip. Add an onboarding nudge. Send an email.'
